canonicalExplanation.summary: `git push origin feature` asks the server to **update one branch** with your commits. The server checks that you're **authenticated**, that the branch isn't **protected** (like main on most teams), and that the update is a **fast-forward**: your commits must sit on top of what's already there. If someone pushed first, you get **rejected (non-fast-forward)**. The fix is to **fetch, integrate, re-test and push again**, not to force. `--force` overwrites others' commits; if you truly must replace your own rewritten branch, use `--force-with-lease`, which refuses when the server has work you haven't seen.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner finishes a feature and runs `git push`, which is rejected. Frustrated, they search online and find `git push --force`. That would have deleted a teammate's commit on the shared branch. A feature branch is pushed to a same-named remote branch after tests, then used to open review without updating protected main directly. In this lesson you'll push a feature branch and safely resolve a rejected update without force-overwriting others.

```predict
{"question": "Your push is rejected as non-fast-forward. What does that mean?", "options": ["The server is broken", "The remote branch has commits you don't have locally"], "answer": 1, "why": "Fetch and integrate them first, then push again."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Branches, merges and conflicts**, **Pull policy** and **Short-lived feature branches**.

sections.heading: The rule: push updates one ref, only as a fast-forward
sections.body:
```bash
npm test                                   # push only tested work.
git push -u origin feature/dark-mode       # create origin/feature/dark-mode and track it.
# ... open a pull request on the hosting site ...

git push                                   # later: rejected (non-fast-forward).
git fetch origin
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/feature/dark-mode   # what a teammate added.
git pull --rebase                          # integrate per the project policy.
npm test
git push                                   # now a fast-forward.

git push --force-with-lease                # only for your own rewritten branch.
```

| Rejection | Meaning | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| non-fast-forward. | remote has commits you lack. | fetch, integrate, test, push. |
| protected branch. | direct pushes to main blocked. | push a feature branch and open a review. |
| authentication failed. | credentials missing or wrong. | fix login or SSH key setup. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Does git push send all your branches?", "answer": "No. It pushes the current branch to its upstream (with the default setting), or exactly the branches you name. Other local branches stay local."}
```

sections.heading: Force is not a fix

includes: Push a tested feature branch with an upstream and open a review instead of pushing to main.
Resolve non-fast-forward rejections by fetching and integrating; use --force-with-lease only for your own rewritten branch.

outcomes: Push a feature branch and safely resolve a rejected update without force-overwriting others.

examples.title: Pushing the feature for review
examples.situation: A feature branch is pushed to a same-named remote branch after tests, then used to open review without updating protected main directly.
walkthrough: **Pushed after tests:** npm test passes, then git push -u origin feature/dark-mode.
**Same-named remote branch:** origin/feature/dark-mode now exists and local feature tracks it.
**Open review without updating protected main directly:** the pull request targets main; main will change only after approval.
examples.result: The work is shared for review, and main stays protected.

examples.title: The rejected push
examples.situation: A teammate pushed a fix to the shared feature branch. The learner's push is rejected as non-fast-forward.
walkthrough: git fetch, then HEAD..origin/feature shows the teammate's commit.
git pull --rebase replays the learner's commits on top; tests pass.
A plain git push now succeeds, keeping both people's work.
examples.result: Both sets of commits survive, with no force push.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Push uploads all local branches and files, and force push is the normal fix whenever the server rejects an update.
misconceptions.correction: Push updates only the named refs, and only as fast-forwards by default. A rejection means the remote has work you lack; forcing would delete it.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, what would --force have deleted?

analogy.example: Pushing is like **adding pages to a shared binder**. You can only add on top of the latest page. If someone added a page since you last looked, you must read it and put yours after it. Forcing is **ripping out their page** to make yours fit.
limitations: Binders don't have protected sections; repos do (main).
The lease is checking the binder hasn't changed before replacing your own pages.

nearTransfer.prompt: With two clones of a sandbox remote, cause a non-fast-forward rejection on a shared branch, then resolve it without force. Show git log --graph before and after.
expectedEvidence: Both commits present at the end.

farTransfer.prompt: In a sandbox, rebase your own pushed feature branch, then show that --force-with-lease succeeds when nobody else pushed but refuses after a simulated teammate push. Explain why plain --force would be dangerous in the second case.
scaffold: Push from a second clone to simulate a teammate.

remediation.explanation: On any rejection, read the reason and ask: **what does the server have that I don't?** Fetch, look, integrate, test, push. Never reach for --force first.

recap.summary: To push a feature branch safely, test first, push to a same-named remote branch with an upstream, open a review instead of pushing to protected main, and resolve non-fast-forward rejections by fetching, integrating, re-testing and pushing again, reserving --force-with-lease for your own rewritten branch.
